title: Scientists Found Dinosaur Blood. Can We Clone a Dinosaur Now?
description: Animal Secrets #21. A new study (PNAS, 2 Nov 2026) reports fossil red blood cells with traces of heme inside the 115-million-year-old leg bones of Aratasaurus, a small meat-eating dinosaur from Brazil that even survived a museum fire. We count down five things from deep time that should have rotted away, from 2-million-year-old DNA to a soft T. rex bone and a dinosaur still holding its last meal, and answer the Jurassic Park question honestly. Part of the Wild Sketchbook.

scenes.say: Scientists say they found dinosaur blood. And it's 115 million years old.

scenes.label: Real blood cells?
scenes.say: Not a picture of blood. Not a stain. Tiny fossil red blood cells, still packed inside a bone.

scenes.label: Answer at the end
scenes.say: And at the very end, I'll answer the question everyone's asking. Could this blood bring a dinosaur back?
Okay, so here's the thing. When an animal dies, the soft stuff goes first. Skin, muscle, blood. Gone in weeks.

scenes.label: Bones turned to stone
scenes.say: That's why almost every dinosaur you've ever seen is just bones turned to stone. Rock in the shape of an animal.

scenes.label: 5 things that survived
scenes.say: But sometimes, nature breaks its own rules. So today, five things from deep time that should have rotted away. And didn't.
Each one is older or stranger than the one before. And number one was published in a science journal just this month.

scenes.label: Oldest DNA ever
scenes.say: Number five. The oldest DNA ever read. And it wasn't inside a bone. It was in dirt.

scenes.label: Polar desert
scenes.say: This is far north Greenland. Today it's a frozen polar desert. Almost nothing grows here.

scenes.label: ~2 million years
scenes.say: But in 2022, scientists pulled DNA out of mud layers there. And they dated it to about two million years old.

scenes.label: Mastodons in Greenland
scenes.say: That DNA showed a lost forest. Poplar and birch trees, reindeer, geese. And even mastodons, big cousins of elephants.
Two million years. That beat the old DNA record by about a million years. So why does that matter for dinosaurs?

scenes.label: 158 moa bones
scenes.say: Because DNA falls apart like a clock. Scientists measured it in 158 bones of the moa, a giant extinct bird.

scenes.label: Half-life: 521 years
scenes.say: They found that half of the DNA bonds break in about 521 years. Then half of what's left breaks again. And again.

scenes.label: Max ~6.8 million yrs
scenes.say: Even frozen at minus five degrees, they estimated every bond would be gone after 6.8 million years at most.
Hold on to that number. Because dinosaur bones are tens of millions of years old. Remember that for the ending.

scenes.label: Soft T. rex?
scenes.say: Number four. A Tyrannosaurus rex leg bone that turned out to be soft inside.

scenes.label: 68 million years
scenes.say: In 2005, paleontologist Mary Schweitzer was studying a T. rex thigh bone from Montana. It was about 68 million years old.

scenes.label: Dissolve the rock
scenes.say: Her team soaked pieces of it in weak chemicals to dissolve the rock minerals away. Just to see what was left.

scenes.label: Stretchy vessels
scenes.say: And what was left was stretchy. See-through, bendy tubes that looked just like tiny blood vessels.

scenes.label: Red-brown blobs
scenes.say: Inside them were little round blobs, dark red to brown. She thought they might be red blood cells.

scenes.label: 'Never dreamed I'd see'
scenes.say: Her reaction? "This is not something I ever dreamed I'd see." And honestly, a lot of scientists didn't believe her.
Remember her name. Because Mary Schweitzer comes back at number one, and she isn't on the side you'd expect.

scenes.label: Tail in amber
scenes.say: Number three. A dinosaur tail, feathers and all, trapped in amber like a bug.

scenes.label: Amber market, 2015
scenes.say: In 2015, a scientist named Lida Xing was walking through an amber market in Myanmar. Then he spotted something weird.

scenes.label: Almost a necklace
scenes.say: Sellers thought it was a bit of plant. It was probably going to become jewelry. Somebody's necklace.

scenes.label: 99 million years
scenes.say: But scans showed tiny bones. It was the tail of a small feathered dinosaur, about 99 million years old.

scenes.label: Brown on top
scenes.say: And the feathers still had color clues. Chestnut brown on top, pale or white underneath.

scenes.label: Iron from blood
scenes.say: Here's the twist. Tests found traces of iron in the soft tissue. The team said it was a relic of hemoglobin. Blood chemistry.
So yes, amber really can hold dinosaur stuff. Just not a mosquito full of dinosaur DNA, like in the movies. Not yet, anyway.
Okay, quick question for you. Would you rather see a whole dinosaur or just its blood? Tell me in the comments.
And if you like this kind of thing, subscribe. One animal secret a day, and the next one is already drawn.

scenes.label: The 'statue' dinosaur
scenes.say: Number two. The dinosaur so perfect, people call it a statue. Or a sleeping dragon.

scenes.label: March 21, 2011
scenes.say: March 21, 2011. Canada. A shovel operator named Shawn Funk was digging in an oil sands mine.

scenes.label: Diamond pattern
scenes.say: His bucket hit something hard, with a strange diamond pattern on it. It was skin. Armored dinosaur skin.

scenes.label: 5.5 m, 1.5 tons
scenes.say: It was a nodosaur, a tank-like plant eater. About 5.5 meters long and roughly 1.5 tons.

scenes.label: ~110 million years
scenes.say: About 110 million years ago, it died, washed out to sea, sank, and got sealed in mud on the seafloor.

scenes.label: 7,000 hours
scenes.say: Then one museum technician, Mark Mitchell, spent about 7,000 hours freeing it from the rock. That's around five and a half years.
His reward? The dinosaur is named after him. Borealopelta markmitchelli.

scenes.label: Still in its skin
scenes.say: And because it was sealed so fast, its skin and armor are still in place. It looks like it fell asleep.

scenes.label: Reddish-brown
scenes.say: Scientists even found pigment. On top, it was reddish brown. Underneath, lighter. Camouflage, on an animal built like a tank.

scenes.label: Last meal: ferns
scenes.say: Then they found its stomach. Its last meal was still inside. Mostly ferns.

scenes.label: 88% leaves
scenes.say: About 88 percent was chewed-up leaves. And there was charcoal in there, like it was eating in a forest that had recently burned.
A dinosaur with its skin, its colors, and its dinner. You'd think nothing could beat that. But number one has something even more personal.

scenes.label: Aratasaurus
scenes.say: Number one. The blood of a meat-eating dinosaur from Brazil.

scenes.label: 3 m, 34 kg
scenes.say: It's called Aratasaurus. Scientists estimate it was about three meters long and weighed about 34 kilograms. Small, for a meat eater.

scenes.label: Found in 2008
scenes.say: Its leg bones were dug out of a mine in northeast Brazil in 2008. Then they went to Brazil's National Museum.

scenes.label: Museum fire, 2018
scenes.say: And in 2018, a giant fire destroyed that museum and huge parts of its collection. This fossil survived.

scenes.label: 'Born from fire'
scenes.say: That's even in its name. Aratasaurus means lizard born from fire.

scenes.label: Published Nov 2
scenes.say: Now, on November 2nd, a team led by Kliti Grice in Australia published what they found inside its bones.

scenes.label: 23 microns
scenes.say: Inside the tiny channels where blood vessels once ran, there were round structures. About 23 microns long. The size of a cell.

scenes.label: 14 tries before
scenes.say: And people have tried this before. At least 14 earlier studies claimed blood cells in very old fossils. None of them convinced the experts.

scenes.label: Or contamination?
scenes.say: The problem is always the same. Is it really the animal, or contamination that crept in later?

scenes.label: ~30 tests
scenes.say: But round blobs aren't proof. Minerals can fake that shape. So the team ran almost thirty different tests.

scenes.label: Heme found
scenes.say: And they found heme. That's the iron-holding molecule in your own blood. It's what helps carry oxygen.

scenes.label: Microbe mat
scenes.say: Here's the clever part. This dinosaur was buried under a mat of microbes, and microbes make chlorophyll, which looks a lot like heme.

scenes.label: 300 to 1
scenes.say: In the microbe mat, chlorophyll beat heme by more than 300 to one. But inside the bone? Heme won.

scenes.label: Not everyone agrees
scenes.say: Kliti Grice called it astonishing. A landmark discovery. But here's the plot twist I promised. Not everyone agrees.

scenes.label: Schweitzer: 'not convinced'
scenes.say: Remember Mary Schweitzer? The T. rex scientist? She says she's not convinced these are red blood cells.

scenes.label: No nucleus?
scenes.say: Her reason: bird and crocodile blood cells have a nucleus in the middle. These structures don't show one. And they're bigger.

scenes.label: Maybe a mineral
scenes.say: Another expert thinks the heme is real, but the round shapes might just be blobs of a manganese mineral.

scenes.label: Lab test needed
scenes.say: One expert says the real proof would be to recreate this kind of fossil in a lab. Nobody has done that yet.

scenes.label: 'Controversy welcomed'
scenes.say: And even the team's own museum partner said it out loud. There will be controversy, which is welcomed. That's how science works.

scenes.label: Clone a dinosaur?
scenes.say: So. Can this blood bring a dinosaur back? Here's the honest answer. No.

scenes.label: Heme isn't DNA
scenes.say: Heme isn't DNA. They're different molecules. Finding one doesn't mean the other survived. And this study found no DNA.

scenes.label: 50x older
scenes.say: Remember, the oldest DNA ever read is about two million years old. This blood is more than fifty times older.

scenes.label: Why blood matters
scenes.say: So why care about old blood at all? Because blood cells can show how an animal lived. How it breathed, and how it handled its world.
But it still tells us something wild. Real pieces of dinosaurs can hide inside bones for 115 million years.

scenes.label: Comment your number
scenes.say: So which one blew your mind most? The blood, the soft T. rex, or the dinosaur with its last meal? Comment your number.

short.title: This Dinosaur Bone Still Had Blood Cells Inside
short.description: Scientists report fossil red blood cells with traces of heme inside the leg bones of Aratasaurus, a 115-million-year-old dinosaur from Brazil (PNAS, Nov 2026). Some experts aren't convinced, and no DNA was found. The full countdown of 5 things that survived deep time is on the channel. Part of the Wild Sketchbook.

scenes.say: This dinosaur bone still has blood inside it. Really. After 115 million years.

scenes.label: Inside the bone
scenes.say: In its leg bones, tiny round structures, about the size of a cell, packed into old blood vessel channels.

scenes.label: Heme found
scenes.say: Almost thirty tests later, they found heme. That's the iron molecule in your blood that carries oxygen.

scenes.label: Survived a fire
scenes.say: And this fossil already survived a giant museum fire in 2018. Its name literally means lizard born from fire.

scenes.label: Not everyone agrees
scenes.say: But some experts aren't convinced. Bird blood cells have a nucleus, and these show no sign of one. Could it be a mineral?

scenes.label: Clone it? No
scenes.say: And no, you can't clone it. No DNA was found. Dinosaur DNA is long gone.

scenes.say: So is it real? Scientists are still arguing. All because a team says this dinosaur bone
